title: Neuron and Nerve Histology
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the microscopic organization of nervous tissue: the parts and shapes of neurons, the connective tissue wrappings of a peripheral nerve, the glial cells that myelinate, support, defend, and line the nervous system, and the way neurons and axons respond to injury. Board questions usually show a cell or a lesion and ask you to name the cell involved, the disease that targets it, or what happens after an axon is cut or a neuron loses its oxygen supply. Knowing why the axon hillock lacks Nissl substance, why one oligodendrocyte matters more than one Schwann cell, and why peripheral axons regrow answers most questions here.

connections.how: Neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependyma come from the neural tube, while Schwann cells and sensory ganglion neurons come from neural crest.
Myelin, nodes of Ranvier, and the axon initial segment explain where action potentials start and how fast they travel.
Multiple sclerosis and the leukodystrophies are diseases of oligodendrocytes and CNS myelin described here at the cell level.
Red neurons, liquefactive necrosis, and gliosis are the tissue stages of ischemic stroke and global hypoxia.
Wallerian degeneration, Schwann cell tubes, and the nerve sheaths decide whether a crushed or cut nerve recovers.

sections.title: Parts of a neuron and the three neuron shapes

blocks.text: A neuron is built to receive signals, decide whether to fire, and send the result over a long distance. The large lower motor neuron of the spinal cord anterior horn shows every part clearly, so it is the standard example. Its soma (cell body) contains a large, pale, euchromatic nucleus with a prominent nucleolus, a sign of very active protein synthesis.

The soma cytoplasm is filled with Nissl substance, which is stacked rough endoplasmic reticulum and free polyribosomes. Ribosomal RNA binds basic dyes such as cresyl violet, so Nissl substance appears as dark blue clumps. It extends into the proximal dendrites but is absent from the axon hillock and the axon, so the hillock looks pale on a Nissl stain. This tells you the axon makes little protein of its own; it depends on axonal transport, with kinesin carrying cargo toward the terminal (anterograde) and dynein carrying cargo back to the soma (retrograde). Retrograde transport is also the route by which tetanus toxin, rabies virus, and herpes simplex virus reach the cell body.

blocks.text: Synaptic input on dendrites and soma spreads passively, and the neuron fires only if the summed depolarization reaches threshold at the initial segment.
Neuron shapes

Neurons are classified by the number of processes that leave the soma. Multipolar neurons have one axon and many dendrites and make up motor neurons, autonomic ganglion neurons, and most CNS neurons. Pseudounipolar neurons begin as bipolar cells in development; the two processes fuse near the soma, leaving one stem that divides in a T into a peripheral branch running to a receptor and a central branch entering the spinal cord or brainstem. Both branches are structurally axons, so the impulse can pass from one to the other without crossing the soma. Their round somas sit in dorsal root ganglia and cranial sensory ganglia, each surrounded by a ring of satellite cells. Bipolar neurons have one dendrite and one axon at opposite poles and are found in special sensory pathways.

blocks.title: Neuron shapes and where they are found
rows: Anterior horn motor neurons, autonomic ganglia, most CNS neurons
One stem dividing into peripheral and central branches
Dorsal root ganglia, most cranial sensory ganglia
Impulse bypasses the soma; mesencephalic nucleus of CN V is a CNS exception
Retinal bipolar cells, olfactory receptor neurons, spiral and vestibular ganglia
Olfactory neurons are replaced from basal stem cells throughout life
blocks.caption: Shape predicts function: many inputs for integration, a direct path for sensation, a simple relay for special senses.

blocks.predict: A section stained with cresyl violet shows a large neuron with one pale cone-shaped region leaving the soma. Which part is it, and why is it pale?
blocks.explain: It is the axon hillock. It lacks rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes, so there is no RNA to take up the basic dye, whereas the soma and dendrites stain blue.

sections.title: Connective tissue layers of a peripheral nerve and the blood-nerve barrier

blocks.text: A peripheral nerve is a bundle of axons, each with its Schwann cells, organized by three connective tissue sheaths. Reading from inside out, the endoneurium surrounds each nerve fiber, the perineurium surrounds each fascicle (a bundle of fibers), and the epineurium surrounds the whole nerve.

blocks.title: The three sheaths of a peripheral nerve
rows: Each nerve fiber (axon plus Schwann cell)
Loose connective tissue with thin collagen and reticular fibers, fibroblasts, capillaries; lies outside the Schwann cell basal lamina
Supports fibers; holds endoneurial fluid and capillaries
Several concentric layers of flattened epithelioid cells, each layer with basal lamina and tight junctions
Diffusion barrier; part of the blood-nerve barrier
Whole nerve and spaces between fascicles
Dense irregular connective tissue with type I collagen and fat
Protects against stretch and compression; carries the vasa nervorum
blocks.caption: Endo, peri, epi: fiber, fascicle, whole nerve.

blocks.text: The perineurium is the most specialized layer. Its cells behave like an epithelium: they rest on basal laminae and are sealed to one another by tight junctions, so substances in the surrounding tissue cannot diffuse freely into the fascicle. This keeps the endoneurial fluid around the axons stable in ionic composition and protects axons from toxins, drugs, and infectious agents. The perineurium also gives the fascicle much of its tensile strength.

The blood-nerve barrier has two parts. The perineurium blocks entry from the surrounding tissue, and the endoneurial capillaries, which are continuous (nonfenestrated) and joined by tight junctions, block entry from the blood. Together they are the peripheral counterpart of the blood-brain barrier. The barrier is weaker in the dorsal root ganglia and at the nerve roots, where capillaries are more permeable. This helps explain why some neurotoxins and immune attacks concentrate in sensory ganglia and roots, as in the root inflammation of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

At the spinal and cranial roots the sheaths are continuous with the meninges: the epineurium with the dura mater and the perineurium with the arachnoid. The epineurial vasa nervorum feed the nerve, so diseases of small vessels, such as diabetic microangiopathy and vasculitis, cause ischemic damage to nerves.
Why the sheaths matter after injury

The layers that survive an injury decide how well the nerve recovers. If the endoneurial tubes and Schwann cell basal laminae stay intact, regenerating axons are guided back to their original targets. If the perineurium and epineurium are cut through, axons sprout into scar tissue and may form a painful neuroma or reach the wrong target.

blocks.title: Seddon classification of nerve injury

Complete, usually within weeks once myelin is repaired
Axon cut; endoneurial tubes and outer sheaths intact (typical crush)

Poor; without guidance tubes, axons form a neuroma or reach the wrong target
blocks.caption: The more connective tissue that survives, the better the guidance for regrowth.

sections.title: Schwann cells, oligodendrocytes, and diseases of myelin

blocks.text: Myelin is glial plasma membrane wrapped many times around an axon and compacted, about 70 to 80% lipid (cholesterol, galactocerebroside, sphingomyelin). Two cell types make it, and the difference between them explains the pattern of each demyelinating disease.

blocks.title: Schwann cells versus oligodendrocytes
rows: Internodes on many axons, up to about 50
One nonmyelinating cell wraps several small axons (C fibers)
Proteolipid protein, myelin basic protein, MOG
blocks.caption: One-to-one in the PNS, one-to-many in the CNS.

blocks.text: Myelin speeds conduction by acting as electrical insulation. It raises the resistance across the internodal membrane and lowers its capacitance, so less current leaks out and less charge is spent changing membrane voltage. Current therefore spreads passively and quickly along the internode to the next node of Ranvier, where voltage-gated Na+ channels are clustered at very high density.

blocks.title: Saltatory conduction
steps: Action potential opens dense Na+ channels at a node
Inward current spreads rapidly along the insulated internode
Next node depolarizes to threshold and fires
Impulse jumps node to node at high velocity
blocks.caption: Only the nodes regenerate the action potential; the internode conducts passively.

blocks.text: When myelin is lost, current leaks across the bare internode, whose membrane has few Na+ channels, so the next node is reached slowly (slowing) or not at all (conduction block). Block causes weakness and sensory loss; uneven slowing desynchronizes the volley and abolishes tendon reflexes. Demyelinated axons are also heat sensitive because Na+ channels inactivate faster at higher temperature, so MS symptoms worsen with a hot bath or fever (Uhthoff phenomenon).

Guillain-Barré syndrome, in its classic demyelinating form, is an acute immune attack on Schwann cell myelin, often 1 to 3 weeks after Campylobacter jejuni enteritis or a viral illness. The mechanism is molecular mimicry (microbial antigens resembling nerve components), and macrophages strip myelin from internodes. Root inflammation raises CSF protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation). The result is ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia, sparing the CNS.

Multiple sclerosis is a T cell mediated autoimmune attack on CNS myelin and oligodendrocytes, producing plaques in periventricular white matter, optic nerves, brainstem, and spinal cord, with oligoclonal IgG bands in the CSF. Because one oligodendrocyte supports many axons, each lost cell demyelinates many fibers, and remyelination is incomplete. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is lytic JC polyomavirus infection of oligodendrocytes when cellular immunity fails (advanced HIV, transplant immunosuppression, or natalizumab, which blocks lymphocyte entry into the CNS). Infected oligodendrocytes have enlarged nuclei with ground-glass inclusions, and multifocal white matter lesions follow.

blocks.title: Demyelinating versus axonal nerve injury on nerve conduction studies
blocks.text: Two patients have leg weakness. In patient A, motor conduction velocity is 25 m/s (normal is roughly 40 m/s or more), distal latency is prolonged, and the response is much smaller with proximal than with distal stimulation. In patient B, velocity is 42 m/s but the response is small. Velocity depends on myelin, so marked slowing with focal block means damaged internodes: patient A has a demyelinating neuropathy such as classic Guillain-Barré syndrome. Amplitude reflects how many axons conduct, so a small response at near-normal speed means axon loss with intact myelin on the survivors: patient B has an axonal neuropathy.

blocks.predict: Why does a small MS plaque often cause more deficit than loss of a similar number of Schwann cells?
blocks.explain: One oligodendrocyte myelinates internodes on many axons, so its loss demyelinates many fibers, and CNS remyelination is limited. Each Schwann cell serves one internode, and surviving Schwann cells can remyelinate.

blocks.text: Astrocytes are the most numerous glial cells. They arise from neuroectoderm and contain glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), an intermediate filament used to identify them and their tumors. Protoplasmic astrocytes lie in gray matter and fibrous astrocytes in white matter. Their processes contact synapses, nodes of Ranvier, and capillaries, and neighboring astrocytes are linked by gap junctions into a network.

The blood-brain barrier itself is formed by brain capillary endothelium: continuous, nonfenestrated cells joined by tight junctions, with few transport vesicles. Astrocyte end-feet cover nearly the whole capillary surface and, with pericytes, induce and maintain these endothelial properties. The end-feet carry aquaporin-4 water channels, the target of the antibody in neuromyelitis optica, which links an astrocyte protein to a demyelinating disease.

Astrocytes also control the fluid around neurons. Each action potential releases K+ into the small extracellular space, and if K+ accumulated it would depolarize nearby neurons. Astrocytes take up K+ through inward rectifier channels (Kir4.1), pass it through gap junctions, and release it where concentration is lower, often near capillaries; this is spatial buffering. They also remove synaptic glutamate with high-affinity transporters, convert it to glutamine with glutamine synthetase, and return glutamine to neurons. Because this enzyme is also the brain's main way to detoxify ammonia, hyperammonemia in liver failure loads astrocytes with glutamine, causing swelling and Alzheimer type II astrocytes.

blocks.title: Spatial buffering of potassium
steps: Repeated firing raises extracellular K+ near active neurons
Astrocytes take up K+ through Kir4.1 channels
K+ moves through gap junctions across the astrocyte network
K+ is released at end-feet near capillaries
Extracellular K+ falls; neuronal excitability returns to normal
blocks.caption: Failure of this system lowers seizure threshold.

blocks.text: After injury, astrocytes enlarge, proliferate, and increase GFAP, a response called reactive gliosis. Because the brain parenchyma has almost no fibroblasts, the glial scar is the CNS form of scarring. It walls off damaged tissue and restores the barrier, but its proteoglycans also block axonal regrowth (C05).

Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS. Unlike the other glia, they are of myeloid (mesodermal) origin, derived from yolk sac progenitors that colonize the brain early in development. At rest they have small elongated nuclei and branched processes; when activated they phagocytose debris and present antigen on MHC class II. In HIV encephalitis, the virus enters microglia and perivascular macrophages through CD4 and the CCR5 coreceptor, and infected cells fuse through viral envelope proteins into multinucleated giant cells within microglial nodules. Neurons are not infected; they are injured by cytokines and viral proteins released from these cells.

Ependymal cells are ciliated cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells that line the ventricles and central canal of the spinal cord. Their cilia help move CSF, and the junctions between them are leaky, so CSF and brain extracellular fluid exchange freely. Over the choroid plexus, modified ependymal cells sealed by tight junctions secrete CSF and form the blood-CSF barrier.

sections.title: Axon transection: Wallerian degeneration, chromatolysis, and regeneration

blocks.text: Because the axon has no ribosomes, everything it needs comes from the soma by axonal transport. When an axon is cut, the distal segment loses that supply and dies, while the cell body survives and attempts repair.

Distal to the cut, the axon undergoes Wallerian degeneration. For a few days the distal stump still conducts, then the axon swells and breaks into fragments and its myelin collapses into ovoids. This is an active process: loss of a short-lived survival enzyme (NMNAT2) supplied by the soma triggers a self-destruct program that depletes NAD+. In the PNS, Schwann cells stop making myelin, begin breaking it down, and recruit macrophages, so debris is cleared within weeks. Proximal to the cut, the axon degenerates only back to the nearest node or two.

In the cell body, central chromatolysis begins within 1 to 2 days and peaks at about 1 to 3 weeks. The soma swells and rounds, Nissl substance disperses from the center toward the periphery, and the nucleus moves to the edge of the cell. The rough endoplasmic reticulum is not lost; it is reorganized as the neuron shifts from making neurotransmitter-related proteins to making structural proteins such as tubulin and actin for regrowth. Chromatolysis is reversible if the axon reconnects; if it does not, the neuron may atrophy or die.

blocks.title: Peripheral axon injury and regrowth
steps: Axon is cut; distal segment loses transport from the soma

Schwann cells and macrophages clear debris
Cell body shows central chromatolysis and makes growth proteins
Schwann cells proliferate in basal lamina tubes (bands of Büngner)

Axon reaches target; Schwann cells remyelinate it
blocks.caption: Regrowth depends on surviving endoneurial tubes and Schwann cells.

blocks.text: Peripheral axons regrow because the environment supports them. Denervated Schwann cells divide inside the preserved basal lamina tubes, forming bands of Büngner, and secrete neurotrophic factors such as nerve growth factor and adhesive molecules such as laminin. Sprouts from the proximal stump enter these tubes and grow at about 1 mm per day, roughly 2.5 cm (1 inch) per month. Regenerated internodes are shorter and thinner, so conduction velocity usually stays somewhat below normal. Axons that enter the wrong tube reach the wrong target, which explains synkinesis after facial nerve injury.

blocks.title: Why PNS axons regrow and CNS axons generally do not
rows: Schwann cells dedifferentiate, divide, and guide
Oligodendrocytes do not form guidance tubes
Slow; myelin debris persists for months
Myelin proteins (Nogo-A, MAG, OMgp) and glial scar proteoglycans
Useful regrowth if tubes are aligned
blocks.caption: Adult CNS neurons also have less intrinsic capacity to grow, so CNS injuries leave permanent deficits even when cell bodies survive.

blocks.title: Estimating recovery time after a nerve injury
blocks.text: A crush of the ulnar nerve at the elbow leaves the endoneurial tubes intact (axonotmesis). The first dorsal interosseous lies roughly 30 cm (300 mm) away along the nerve. At about 1 mm per day, regrowth takes about 300 days, roughly 10 months, plus a short delay to cross the injury site. Denervated muscle and motor end plates deteriorate over roughly 12 to 18 months, so the hand muscles are reinnervated close to that limit and recovery is often incomplete. Distance from target, not only severity, predicts outcome.

sections.title: Red neurons and acute hypoxic-ischemic neuronal injury

blocks.text: Neurons are the cells most sensitive to loss of oxygen and glucose. They depend almost entirely on oxidative phosphorylation, store little glycogen, and spend a large share of their ATP running the Na+/K+-ATPase. A few minutes of complete ischemia can start irreversible injury, but the light microscope cannot show that injury until about 12 to 24 hours later, when red neurons appear.

blocks.title: Hypoxic-ischemic neuronal injury
steps: Ischemia stops oxidative phosphorylation; ATP falls
Na+/K+-ATPase fails; neuron depolarizes
Glutamate is released and not taken back up
NMDA receptors open; Ca2+ floods the neuron
Ca2+ activates proteases, phospholipases, and nitric oxide synthase
Mitochondria fail; free radicals form
Red neurons visible about 12 to 24 hours later
blocks.caption: Excess glutamate signaling (excitotoxicity) links energy failure to Ca2+ overload.

blocks.text: A red neuron is shrunken and angular, with intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm, a small dark pyknotic nucleus, loss of the nucleolus, and loss of Nissl substance. Each feature has a cause. Nissl substance is basophilic because of its RNA, and when ribosomes break down the cytoplasm loses its blue tint. Denatured cytoplasmic proteins then bind eosin strongly, so the cell looks bright red. The nucleus condenses (pyknosis) as chromatin collapses, a sign that the cell is dead rather than injured.

Not all neurons are equally vulnerable. In global hypoxia or hypoperfusion, such as cardiac arrest, the first to die are pyramidal cells of hippocampal sector CA1 (Sommer sector), cerebellar Purkinje cells, and pyramidal neurons in neocortical layers 3, 5, and 6, giving a band-like pattern called pseudolaminar necrosis. These cells receive heavy glutamatergic input and have high metabolic demand. Regional hypoperfusion also targets watershed zones between arterial territories.

blocks.title: Tissue stages after a brain infarct
rows: Acute inflammation at the necrotic tissue
Cyst walled off by glial scar
blocks.caption: Times are approximate and vary with lesion size and source.

blocks.text: The brain undergoes liquefactive necrosis rather than the coagulative necrosis typical of other organs after ischemia, because it is rich in lipid, has little supporting collagen, and is digested by enzymes from microglia and macrophages. Red neurons must also be distinguished from central chromatolysis: chromatolysis is a reversible reaction to axonal injury with a swollen soma and peripheral nucleus, whereas a red neuron is shrunken, eosinophilic, and dead.

blocks.predict: A patient dies 6 hours after cardiac arrest with prolonged resuscitation. Would red neurons be expected in the hippocampus at autopsy?
blocks.explain: Probably not. Irreversible injury has begun, but red neurons usually take about 12 to 24 hours to become visible, so neurons can look normal on routine sections at 6 hours.

integration.text: Embryology and cell biology explain the cell types. Neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependyma come from the neural tube; Schwann cells, satellite cells, and sensory ganglion neurons come from neural crest; microglia are myeloid immigrants. Because the axon lacks ribosomes, it depends on transport from the soma, which is why a cut axon degenerates distally, why viruses and toxins can travel retrograde to the cell body, and why distal axons are the first to fail in many metabolic neuropathies.

Immunology, microbiology, and pathology act on specific cells. Schwann cell myelin is the target in Guillain-Barré syndrome, oligodendrocytes in MS and PML, astrocyte aquaporin-4 in neuromyelitis optica, and microglia in HIV encephalitis. Myelin determines conduction velocity, so demyelination shows as slowing and block while axon loss shows as reduced amplitude. Light microscopy lags behind events: red neurons appear hours after irreversible injury, and nerve conduction distal to a cut stays normal for several days, so timing must be considered before interpreting findings.

summary: Nissl substance (rough ER and ribosomes) fills the soma and dendrites but is absent from the axon hillock and axon, which depend on kinesin and dynein transport.
Action potentials begin at the axon initial segment, where voltage-gated Na+ channels are densest.

Multipolar neurons are motor and most CNS neurons; pseudounipolar neurons sit in dorsal root and cranial sensory ganglia; bipolar neurons serve the retina, olfaction, and the spiral and vestibular ganglia.
Endoneurium surrounds each fiber, perineurium each fascicle, and epineurium the whole nerve; perineurial tight junctions and endoneurial capillaries form the blood-nerve barrier.
Schwann cells (neural crest) myelinate one internode of one axon; oligodendrocytes (neural tube) myelinate many axons, so CNS demyelination spreads widely.
Guillain-Barré syndrome attacks Schwann cell myelin; MS attacks CNS myelin; JC virus kills oligodendrocytes in PML.

Astrocytes induce the blood-brain barrier, buffer K+, recycle glutamate, detoxify ammonia, and form the glial scar; microglia are myeloid macrophages that form giant cells in HIV encephalitis; ependyma lines the ventricles.
Wallerian degeneration occurs distal to a cut, central chromatolysis in the cell body; PNS axons regrow about 1 mm per day along bands of Büngner.
CNS axons rarely regrow because of absent guide tubes, inhibitory myelin proteins, slow debris clearance, and the glial scar.
Red neurons (shrunken, eosinophilic, pyknotic) mark irreversible hypoxic injury about 12 to 24 hours after the insult; CA1, Purkinje cells, and cortical layers 3, 5, and 6 die first.

verify: The maximum number of internodes per oligodendrocyte is quoted from about 40 to 60 in different sources; this chapter says up to about 50.
Regeneration rate is quoted as about 1 mm per day in most review sources and 1 to 3 mm per day in some texts; confirm the value NABNE expects.
The window of about 12 to 18 months before denervated muscle and motor end plates become unreceptive varies between surgical sources.
Timing of infarct stages (neutrophils, macrophages, gliosis) differs slightly among pathology texts; values are stated as approximate.
Continuity of the perineurium with the arachnoid is described in most histology texts, but some describe the perineurium as continuous with the pia-arachnoid; confirm the wording NABNE uses.
Microglial origin is given as yolk sac myeloid progenitors in current sources, while older review books state bone marrow monocytes or simply mesoderm; confirm which NABNE expects.
The NMNAT2 and NAD+ mechanism of Wallerian degeneration is current research consensus but may exceed what NABNE Part I tests.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Sommer sector, bands of Büngner, Uhthoff phenomenon, and Seddon classification, or only the descriptive terms.
